items.prompt: Which punctuation mark is missing? “Where is my bag ___” asked Rudi.

options.text: a full stop
options.why: Rudi is asking a question, so a full stop is not right.

options.text: a comma
options.why: A comma is used when spoken words are a statement, not a question.

options.text: a question mark
an exclamation mark
options.why: An exclamation mark shows strong feeling, but Rudi is asking something.

hints: Read Rudi’s words aloud. What kind of sentence is it?
The punctuation inside the speech marks should match the kind of sentence that is spoken.
Look at the first word Rudi says. Does it start a statement or a question?
items.explanation: Where is my bag is a question, so it ends with a question mark inside the speech marks.

items.prompt: Write only the words that Lia actually said. Lia shouted, “Look at that rainbow!”
hints: The spoken words are inside the speech marks.
Leave out the words that tell us who is speaking.
Find the opening speech mark and copy from there to the closing one.
items.explanation: The words inside the speech marks are what Lia said. Lia shouted is the reporting clause.

options.text: “Can I borrow your ruler,” asked Tono?
options.why: The question mark belongs inside the speech marks, straight after ruler.

options.text: Can I borrow your ruler? asked Tono.
options.why: Speech marks are missing around the spoken words.

options.text: “Can I borrow your ruler?” asked Tono.
“Can I borrow your ruler”? asked Tono.
options.why: The question mark should come before the closing speech mark, not after it.

hints: Check where the speech marks and the question mark are in each sentence.
The punctuation that ends the spoken words goes inside the closing speech mark.
Find the sentence where the question mark comes just before the closing speech mark.
items.explanation: The question is inside the speech marks with its question mark, and asked Tono continues the sentence with a small a.

items.prompt: Where should the comma go? “We are going to the zoo” said Dad.

options.text: after zoo, inside the speech marks
after said
options.why: A comma after said would split the words that tell us who is speaking.

options.text: after Dad
options.why: The sentence ends after Dad, so it needs a full stop there.

options.text: before We
options.why: Nothing comes before the speech, so no comma is needed there.

hints: The spoken words are a statement, and the sentence carries on after them.
When speech comes first, a comma separates it from the words that say who spoke.
Find the last spoken word. What should come straight after it?
items.explanation: When the spoken words come first and the sentence continues, a comma goes inside the closing speech marks: “We are going to the zoo,” said Dad.

items.prompt: Choose 2 rules for writing direct speech.

options.text: Start a new line when a new person speaks.
Put the spoken words inside speech marks.
End all speech with a full stop outside the speech marks.
options.why: Punctuation that ends the spoken words goes inside the speech marks.

options.text: Use a capital letter for every spoken word.
options.why: Only the first spoken word and names need capital letters.

options.text: Never use a question mark in speech.
options.why: Questions in speech need question marks inside the speech marks.

hints: Think about what a page of dialogue in a story looks like.
Check each rule against a speech sentence you know is correct.
Start with the rule about speech marks. Is it true?
items.explanation: Spoken words go inside speech marks, and each new speaker starts on a new line. This helps the reader follow who is talking.

items.prompt: “I am tired,” said Maya. Finish the reported speech: Maya said that she ___ tired.
hints: In reported speech, we tell what someone said without speech marks.
The verb usually moves one step into the past.
Maya said am. What is the past tense of am?
items.explanation: In reported speech, am changes to was because Maya said it in the past: Maya said that she was tired.

items.prompt: Sort the sentences into direct speech and reported speech.

items.text: Dina said that she loved mangoes.
The coach told us to warm up.
Arif asked if the bus had left.

hints: Direct speech shows the exact words that were said.
Look for speech marks. Reported speech does not use them.
Start with the first sentence. Does it have speech marks?
items.explanation: Direct speech uses speech marks around the exact words. Reported speech retells the words without speech marks, often with that or if.

items.prompt: Which is the correct reported speech? “I will help you tomorrow,” Ben told me.

options.text: Ben told me that I would help him the next day.
options.why: The pronouns are swapped. Ben is the one who will help.

options.text: Ben told me that he would help me the next day.
Ben told me that he would help you tomorrow.
options.why: You should change to me, because Ben was speaking to me.

options.text: Ben told me, “he would help me the next day.”
options.why: Reported speech does not use speech marks.

hints: Think about who is speaking and who is being helped.
In reported speech, I and you change to fit the person telling the story, and will changes to would.
Ben said I. When you retell it, who is that I?
items.explanation: Ben’s I becomes he, you becomes me, will becomes would and tomorrow becomes the next day.

items.prompt: Which is the correct reported speech? “Did you finish your homework?” Mum asked me.

options.text: Mum asked me did I finish my homework?
options.why: Reported questions are written as statements, without a question mark.

options.text: Mum asked me if you had finished your homework.
options.why: You should change to I, because Mum was asking me.

options.text: Mum asked me if I had finished my homework.
Mum asked me, if I had finished my homework?
options.why: There should be no comma before if, and no question mark.

hints: A reported question is no longer a direct question.
Reported questions often use if, change the pronouns and end with a full stop.
Start with Mum asked me if. Who is the I in the rest of the sentence?
items.explanation: A yes or no question is reported with if. You becomes I, did you finish becomes had finished, and the sentence ends with a full stop.

items.prompt: Which is the correct reported speech? “We visited this museum yesterday,” said the twins.

options.text: The twins said that we visited this museum yesterday.
options.why: We should change to they, and the time and place words should change too.

options.text: The twins said that they had visited that museum the day before.
The twins said that they visited this museum yesterday.
options.why: In reported speech, this usually becomes that and yesterday becomes the day before.

options.text: The twins said that they had visited this museum the day after.
options.why: Yesterday means the day before, not the day after.

hints: Several words in the sentence need to change.
Check the pronoun, the verb, the word this and the time word one at a time.
Start with the pronoun. The twins said we. Who is we when you retell it?
items.explanation: We becomes they, visited becomes had visited, this becomes that and yesterday becomes the day before.
